docs.title: fastapi-bedrock
docs.text:
The solid, layered foundation you build your FastAPI service on.

A Cookiecutter template for production-ready FastAPI services organised with a Domain-Driven Design (vertical-slice) layout. Every generated project ships fully wired: async database access, a clean repository/service layering, JWT authentication, tests against a real PostgreSQL, linting, strict typing, Docker and CI — nothing to bolt on afterwards.

Not related to Amazon Bedrock

Bedrock here means what it says on the tin — the solid layer of rock you build on. This project is a template for FastAPI backend services and has no connection to AWS's Amazon Bedrock LLM platform.

docs.title: Why this template
docs.text:
• Backend-first. No frontend to delete. The output is an API service the way platform and microservice teams actually deploy them.
  • Composable. Nine use_* flags add or remove whole modules — auth, Docker, CI, rate limiting, Sentry, Temporal, Redis, OpenTelemetry, an outbound HTTP client — and every combination is exercised in the template's own CI matrix. See the options matrix.
  • Opinionated where it pays. Repository → service → router layering, RFC 9457 problem+json errors, refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, a transactional outbox for events, structlog JSON logging with request IDs. See architecture.
  • Updatable. Generate with cruft and later pull template improvements into your project as a reviewable diff. See upgrading.
  • Tested like production. pytest + testcontainers run the suite against a real PostgreSQL — no SQLite stand-in — and mypy --strict covers src and tests.

docs.title: The stack
docs.text: Concern Choice Language Python 3.12 / 3.13 / 3.14 Packaging / env uv (PEP 621 + PEP 735) Web framework FastAPI Data / ORM SQLModel on SQLAlchemy 2.0 async — PostgreSQL / asyncpg Migrations Alembic (async) Validation / config Pydantic v2 + pydantic-settings Auth OAuth2 password flow, JWT access + refresh, Argon2 (pwdlib) Lint + format Ruff Type checking mypy (strict, incl. tests) Tests pytest, httpx, polyfactory, testcontainers Logging structlog (JSON) + request IDs Runtime extras Docker + compose, CI, rate limiting, Sentry, Temporal, Redis, OTel/Grafana

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The generated project follows a repository → service → router flow with each domain as a self-contained vertical slice.

flowchart LR
    client((Client)) --> mw["middleware<br>request-id, security headers,<br>CORS, body-size limit"]
    mw --> api["api router<br>/api/v1"]
    api --> health["/health, /ready"]
    api --> auth["auth router (JWT)"]
    api --> dom["<entity> router"]
    auth --> asvc["auth service"]
    dom --> svc["<entity> service"]
    asvc --> urepo["user repository"]
    svc --> repo["<entity> repository"]
    urepo --> db[(PostgreSQL)]
    repo --> db
    svc -.->|outbox event| stream[(Redis Stream)]
    svc -.->|start workflow| temporal["Temporal"]

Dashed arrows are optional slices (use_redis, use_temporal); the auth slice ships with use_auth=yes.

docs.title: Directory layout
docs.text:
src/<package>/
├── main.py                 # app factory, lifespan, middleware
├── core/                   # cross-cutting infrastructure
│   ├── config.py           # pydantic-settings, fail-fast production checks
│   ├── database.py         # async engine + session dependency
│   ├── repository.py       # generic BaseRepository[Model]
│   ├── security.py         # password hashing + JWT     (use_auth)
│   ├── logging.py          # structlog configuration
│   ├── middleware.py       # request-id middleware
│   └── exceptions.py       # domain errors + RFC 9457 handlers
├── api/
│   ├── router.py           # aggregates every domain router under /api/v1
│   └── health.py           # /health and /ready probes
├── domains/
│   ├── auth/               # User model, JWT login/refresh   (use_auth)
│   └── <entity>/           # models · schemas · repository · service · router
├── events/                 # outbox relay + Streams consumer (use_redis)
└── temporal/               # client, worker, workflows       (use_temporal)

docs.title: The layering rule
docs.text:
Business logic never touches the database directly:

  • Routers own HTTP: request/response schemas, status codes, dependencies.
  • Services own business logic and transactions; they raise typed domain errors (NotFoundError, ConflictError, …) that handlers render as RFC 9457 application/problem+json.
  • Repositories own persistence: thin classes over a generic BaseRepository[Model], so a domain is trivial to unit-test and the persistence layer stays swappable.

Every domain repeats the same five files (models, schemas, repository, service, router), so any slice is navigable once you have read one. make new-domain name=order scaffolds a complete new slice plus tests.

docs.title: Cross-cutting behaviour
docs.text:
• Errors — every error response is an RFC 9457 problem document with a stable type URN; validation failures add a field-level errors array.
  • Logging — structlog emits one JSON request_completed event per request; every response carries an X-Request-ID header.
  • Config — pydantic-settings with fail-fast validation: unsafe production configuration (default SECRET_KEY, DEBUG=true, wildcard ALLOWED_HOSTS) is rejected at boot rather than silently degraded.
  • Migrations — Alembic owns the schema in staging/production; locally, tables auto-create at startup for convenience (DB_AUTO_CREATE, forced off outside local).
  • Events (optional) — the transactional outbox removes the dual-write race: events are written in the same transaction as the domain change and relayed to a Redis Stream in a CloudEvents 1.0 envelope, consumed at-least-once with XACK/XAUTOCLAIM.
  • Workflows (optional) — Temporal for durable, retried, long-running orchestration; the shipped recipe on background work explains when to use BackgroundTasks vs the outbox vs Temporal.

docs.title: Testing philosophy
docs.text: Tests spin up a real PostgreSQL container (testcontainers) and drive the API through an async httpx client — behaviour matches production instead of a SQLite stand-in. mypy --strict covers src and tests, and Ruff enforces lint + format. make check runs everything.

docs.title: Maintainer checklist
docs.text: One-time repository setup that cannot ship as files in the repo — run these with the GitHub CLI as the repository owner. Items are ordered; later ones assume earlier ones are done.

docs.title: 1. Repo metadata (discoverability + Amazon Bedrock disambiguation)
docs.text:
"fastapi bedrock" search results are dominated by AWS Bedrock projects, so the description must disambiguate and the topics must never contain a bare bedrock:

gh repo edit mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock \
  --description "Production-ready FastAPI + DDD cookiecutter template: async SQLModel, JWT auth, Temporal, transactional outbox events, OpenTelemetry. Not related to Amazon Bedrock." \
  --homepage "https://mohandoz.github.io/fastapi-bedrock/"

gh repo edit mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock \
  --add-topic fastapi \
  --add-topic fastapi-template \
  --add-topic fastapi-boilerplate \
  --add-topic cookiecutter \
  --add-topic cookiecutter-template \
  --add-topic python \
  --add-topic domain-driven-design \
  --add-topic sqlmodel \
  --add-topic uv \
  --add-topic cruft

docs.title: 2. Social preview image
docs.text:
No CLI support — generate a 1280×640 PNG from the logo and upload it under Settings → General → Social preview:

# any SVG rasteriser works; e.g. librsvg
brew install librsvg
rsvg-convert -w 1280 -h 640 --keep-aspect-ratio --page-width 1280 --page-height 640 \
  --top 190 --left 280 assets/logo.svg -o /tmp/social-preview.png

docs.title: 3. Enable Discussions
docs.text:
The issue forms route "questions about my generated project" to Discussions, so enable it before publicising the forms:

gh repo edit mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock --enable-discussions

Create a pinned welcome discussion in a Q&A category pointing at the docs site and the issue forms.

docs.title: 4. Activate GitHub Pages (docs site)
docs.text:
The Docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yml) pushes the built mkdocs-material site to the gh-pages branch. After its first successful run on main:

gh api -X POST repos/mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock/pages \
  -f "source[branch]=gh-pages" -f "source[path]=/"

(or Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → gh-pages / root). The site then serves at https://mohandoz.github.io/fastapi-bedrock/, including /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt for AI assistants.

docs.title: 5. Demo repository (continuously rendered showcase)
docs.text:
The Sync demo workflow (.github/workflows/sync-demo.yml) renders the default configuration and force-pushes it to a public demo repo on every merge to main. It is inert until configured:

# 5.1 create the public demo repo
gh repo create mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock-demo --public \
  --description "Rendered default output of the fastapi-bedrock cookiecutter template (auto-synced; do not PR here)"

# 5.2 create a fine-grained PAT (Settings → Developer settings) scoped to
#     ONLY mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock-demo with Contents: Read and write,
#     then store it and the target repo on the template repo:
gh secret set DEMO_REPO_TOKEN --repo mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock
gh variable set DEMO_REPO --repo mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock --body "mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock-demo"

# 5.3 first sync + mark as a template repo ("Use this template" button)
gh workflow run sync-demo.yml --repo mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock
gh repo edit mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock-demo --template

# 5.4 point evaluators at it
gh repo edit mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock-demo \
  --homepage "https://mohandoz.github.io/fastapi-bedrock/" \
  --add-topic fastapi --add-topic fastapi-template --add-topic cookiecutter

Tag pushes (v*) on the template repo are mirrored to the demo repo, so tag-to-tag diffs of the demo double as per-release upgrade notes.

docs.title: 6. One-click deploy listings (from the demo repo)
docs.text:
• Railway — publish a template from the dashboard (https://railway.com/new/template → Create template): one web service built from mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock-demo's Dockerfile plus a PostgreSQL database; set SECRET_KEY, DATABASE_URL (reference the DB plugin) and ENVIRONMENT=staging. Published templates earn a kickback and give the README a "Deploy on Railway" button.
  • Render — add a render.yaml blueprint to the demo repo (a web service from the Dockerfile plus a managed PostgreSQL), then link https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock-demo as a "Deploy to Render" button.

Because the demo repo is force-pushed by the sync workflow, keep such deploy-only files in the template itself (so they survive re-renders) or accept re-adding them after workflow changes.

docs.title: 7. Submit to lists
docs.text:
• PR the template into the Boilerplate section of mjhea0/awesome-fastapi.
  • Answer the recurring "which FastAPI template" threads with the comparison table (README → How it compares) rather than a bare link.

docs.title: 8. Releases
docs.text: Tag releases (git tag v0.x.y && git push --tags) and write release notes against the CHANGELOG; the docs' upgrade guide and the demo-repo tag diffs both key off tags.

docs.title: Options matrix
docs.text: Cookiecutter asks for a handful of identity variables and eleven use_* feature flags. Every flag adds (or removes) a whole module — dependencies, source files, settings, compose services and tests together — and the template's own CI renders and checks the all-on, all-off and mixed combinations on every change, so any answer set produces a working project.

docs.title: Identity variables
docs.text:
Variable Description Default project_name Human-readable name FastAPI DDD Service project_slug Repo/folder name (derived) fastapi-ddd-service package_name Import package (derived) fastapi_ddd_service project_description One-line description — author_name / author_email Used in pyproject.toml and the API contact info — version Initial version 0.1.0 python_version Target Python (3.13 / 3.14 / 3.12) 3.13 first_entity First domain entity (lowercase snake) item

A pre-generation hook validates the answers (e.g. first_entity must be a lowercase snake-case identifier that is not a Python keyword and not auth; python_version must be one of the supported minors) and fails generation early instead of producing a broken project.

docs.title: use_auth — JWT authentication (default: yes)
docs.text:
The full account lifecycle as a domains/auth/ vertical slice:

  • Routes — register, login (OAuth2 password flow), refresh, logout, /me (read/export/delete, GDPR-shaped), password change / forgot / reset, email verification.
  • Tokens — JWT access + refresh with iss/aud binding; refresh tokens rotate atomically, and reuse of a rotated token revokes the whole token family (RFC 6819 reuse detection). Families live in Redis when use_redis=yes, otherwise in a refresh_tokens table. Password changes/resets advance an account version carried by every token, invalidating old sessions and making reset links single-use.
  • Passwords — Argon2 via pwdlib.
  • Email — password-reset and verification emails (core/email.py); full messages are logged only in local development. Other environments emit metadata-only warnings until EMAILS_ENABLED=true.
  • Bootstrap — FIRST_SUPERUSER_EMAIL/FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD create or promote a superuser at startup; OPEN_REGISTRATION=false makes deployments invite-only.
  • Dependencies added — pyjwt, pwdlib[argon2], jinja2.

Disable it for internal services that sit behind a gateway or use mTLS — the first_entity routes are then unprotected.

docs.title: use_docker — containers (default: yes)
docs.text:
• Multi-stage Dockerfile (uv-based, non-root) and docker-compose.yml with PostgreSQL (plus Temporal/Redis/LGTM services when those flags are on), all ports bound to 127.0.0.1.
  • docker compose watch support for edit-and-reload inside containers.
  • deploy/k8s/ production-shaped Kubernetes overlays: migration-first rollout, probes, non-root read-only securityContext, file-mounted secrets and optional Redis/Temporal worker Deployments.
  • A compose-based .devcontainer/ (a single-container devcontainer remains when the flag is off).
  • make db-up, make docker-up, make db-backup / db-restore targets.

Without Docker you point DATABASE_URL at your own PostgreSQL; the test suite still needs a Docker daemon for testcontainers.

docs.title: use_github_actions — CI (default: yes)
docs.text:
• .github/workflows/ci.yml in the generated project: Ruff, mypy, pytest (with the testcontainers PostgreSQL) and, when use_docker=yes, a Docker build smoke test.
  • Dependabot config and the PR template remain even when the flag is off — only the workflows are Actions-specific.

docs.title: use_rate_limiting — slowapi (default: yes)
docs.text:
• Global RATE_LIMIT (default 100/minute) per client IP; register, forgot/reset-password, login, refresh, verification and metered LLM routes carry stricter endpoint-specific limits.
  • Counters are shared across workers via Redis when use_redis=yes, otherwise in-memory per process.
  • Adds slowapi; documents the FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS / --proxy-headers requirements for running behind a proxy.

docs.title: use_sentry — error tracking (default: no)
docs.text: • core/sentry.py initialises sentry-sdk[fastapi] when SENTRY_DSN is set; traces sampling is configurable (SENTRY_TRACES_SAMPLE_RATE).

docs.title: use_temporal — durable workflows (default: no)
docs.text:
• temporal/ module: client, worker (make worker), a demo workflow + activity wired to the first entity, and a router to start it.
  • Workflows stay deterministic; side effects (including DB access) live in activities.
  • With use_docker=yes, compose also starts the Temporal server, Web UI (http://localhost:8080) and a worker container.
  • Adds temporalio.

docs.title: use_redis — cache, outbox events, locks (default: no)
docs.text:
• Cache — typed cache-aside helper (core/cache.py, CacheDep).
  • Distributed lock — core/lock.py for lease-bounded cross-replica mutual exclusion. Work must finish inside the TTL; irreversible exactly-once effects still need fencing/idempotency.
  • Transactional outbox — enqueue_event(session, ...) writes events in the same DB transaction as your domain change; a relay forwards committed rows to a Redis Stream (CloudEvents 1.0 envelope) and a consumer group processes them at-least-once (make events-worker). Poison messages move to a dead-letter stream after REDIS_MAX_DELIVERY_ATTEMPTS.
  • Idempotency-Key — replayable POST responses per the IETF Idempotency-Key draft, snapshots stored in Redis.
  • Upgrades other flags: shared rate-limit counters, Redis-backed refresh-token families, a Redis testcontainer in the test suite.
  • Adds redis[hiredis].

docs.title: use_observability — OpenTelemetry (default: no)
docs.text:
• core/observability.py exports traces, metrics and logs over OTLP (OTEL_ENABLED=true); FastAPI and SQLAlchemy are auto-instrumented, plus Redis and httpx when those flags are also on.
  • With use_docker=yes, compose starts grafana/otel-lgtm — Collector, Loki, Tempo, Prometheus and Grafana pre-provisioned; logs carry trace_id/span_id so Loki links straight to Tempo traces.
  • Adds the opentelemetry-* SDK, OTLP exporter and instrumentation packages.

docs.title: use_http_client — resilient outbound HTTP (default: no)
docs.text:
• core/http.py wraps httpx.AsyncClient with timeouts, retries (via stamina) and a circuit breaker; built once on app.state, injected with HttpClientDep. Retries fire on network errors and 5xx, never 4xx.
  • Adds stamina (httpx already ships via fastapi[standard]).

docs.title: use_mcp — MCP server for AI agents (default: no)
docs.text:
• Mounts a FastMCP v3 server at /mcp (streamable HTTP) with curated tools over the first_entity service layer — list_*, get_* and create_* (src/<package>/mcp/server.py). Tools are hand-picked over services, never auto-generated from every route.
  • With use_auth=yes, requests must carry the same bearer JWT as the REST API (refresh tokens are rejected). Without auth the endpoint is unauthenticated — the pre-gen hook warns against exposing it publicly.
  • Adds fastmcp.

docs.title: use_llm_example — Anthropic LLM domain (default: no)
docs.text:
• Scaffolds domains/llm/: POST /llm/complete (structured output via the Anthropic SDK's messages.parse) and POST /llm/stream (native FastAPI SSE streaming), with settings ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / ANTHROPIC_MODEL / LLM_*.
  • Testing is two-tier: deterministic faked-SDK tests run in CI, plus an opt-in pydantic-evals lane against the live API (make evals). Nothing is required at generation time; the API key is only needed at runtime and for evals.
  • Adds anthropic (runtime) and pydantic-evals (dev).

docs.title: Choosing a combination
docs.text:
You are building… Suggested answers A public API with accounts defaults (use_auth, use_docker, CI, rate limiting) An internal microservice behind a gateway use_auth=no, keep Docker + CI; add use_observability=yes An event-driven service use_redis=yes (outbox + streams), consider use_temporal=yes for long-running orchestration A service calling flaky third parties use_http_client=yes, use_observability=yes A minimal teaching/example project everything no — you still get the DDD slice, tests, Alembic, structlog, Ruff and strict mypy

Flags interact but never conflict: for example use_redis upgrades rate limiting and auth storage when those are enabled, and observability instruments whichever of Redis/httpx are present. Any combination renders, lints, type-checks and passes its tests.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• uv — used both to run the generator (uvx) and to manage the generated project.
  • Docker — the test suite starts a throwaway PostgreSQL via testcontainers, and local development uses a compose-managed database when use_docker=yes.

docs.title: Generate a project
docs.text:
# recommended: cruft, so the project can pull template updates later
uvx cruft create https://github.com/mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock

# plain cookiecutter works too (no update tracking)
uvx cookiecutter gh:mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock

You will be prompted for the project name, author details, target Python version, the name of your first domain entity, and the nine use_* feature flags — the options matrix explains exactly what each one adds.

When generation finishes, a post-generation hook prunes the modules you disabled, initialises a git repository, runs uv sync and makes an initial commit. Set the environment variable SKIP_UV_SYNC=1 to skip dependency installation (you must then run uv sync yourself before the first push, so uv.lock gets committed).

docs.title: Non-interactive generation
docs.text:
Every variable can be supplied on the command line, which is handy for CI and for trying variants quickly:

uvx cookiecutter gh:mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock --no-input \
  project_name="Order Service" \
  use_temporal=yes use_redis=yes use_observability=yes

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
cd <project_slug>
make setup                  # deps, .env (+ generated SECRET_KEY), database, migrations, git hooks
make run                    # uv run fastapi dev  ->  http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs

The interactive API docs live at /docs, health probes at /api/v1/health and /api/v1/ready.

docs.title: The everyday loop
docs.text:
make test                   # pytest against a testcontainers PostgreSQL
make lint                   # ruff check + format check
make typecheck              # mypy --strict (src + tests)
make check                  # all of the above
make new-domain name=order  # scaffold a full vertical slice + tests
make seed                   # fill the local database with demo data

With use_docker=yes, docker compose up --build starts the full stack, and docker compose watch gives an edit-and-reload loop inside Docker.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read the architecture page to understand the layout before adding your first real domain.
  • Skim the recipes — social login, admin UI, background-job guidance, anti-bot verification and passkeys are all written against the generated codebase.
  • If you generated with cruft, note the .cruft.json at the project root: it is what makes template updates possible later.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
Every generated project ships a docs/recipes/ directory: integration guides written against the generated codebase — they name the real modules, settings blocks and service methods, so the diff between the recipe and your project is minimal. They are rendered with your project's package name during generation.

The sources live in the template at {{cookiecutter.project_slug}}/docs/recipes/ (the links below point there; in your generated project the same files are in docs/recipes/ with all placeholders filled in).

docs.title: Shipped in every project
docs.text:
• Background work: which tool? — BackgroundTasks vs the transactional outbox vs Temporal, with a decision table and one worked example of each. Read it before adding any async work.
  • Admin back-office with SQLAdmin — a model-driven admin UI over the existing SQLModel tables.
  • Feature flags with OpenFeature — vendor-neutral flag evaluation wired through the service layer.

docs.title: Shipped when use_auth=yes
docs.text:
• Social login (OAuth / OIDC) with Authlib — "Sign in with Google" alongside the password flow; the service still mints its own JWT pair, so everything downstream is unchanged.
  • Cloudflare Turnstile verification — a ~40-line dependency that shields unauthenticated endpoints (register, forgot-password) from bot abuse; no-ops until a secret key is configured, so it costs nothing in development.
  • Passkeys / WebAuthn readiness — a credential model alongside the existing users table and the registration/authentication flows with py_webauthn, ending in the same token issuance the password flow uses.

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text: Recipes are deliberately documentation, not flags: they keep the template's surface small while showing the exact upgrade path. If you build an integration you think belongs here, contributions are welcome — a good recipe names real files in the generated project, provides complete copy-pasteable code, and explains the trade-offs at the end.

docs.title: Upgrading generated projects with cruft
docs.text: A cookiecutter template normally helps you once, on day one. cruft extends that to the whole life of the project: it records which template commit a project was generated from and can later replay template improvements onto your codebase as a reviewable diff.

docs.title: Generate with cruft
docs.text:
uvx cruft create https://github.com/mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock

This behaves exactly like cookiecutter, plus it writes a .cruft.json at the project root recording the template URL, the answers you gave and the template commit. Commit that file.

Use the full repository URL with cruft; Cookiecutter's gh: shorthand is passed directly to Git and treated as an SSH hostname.

docs.title: Check and update
docs.text:
uvx cruft check    # exit 1 if the project is behind the template
uvx cruft diff     # preview what an update would change
uvx cruft update   # apply upstream template changes as a local diff

cruft update re-renders the old and new template revisions with your recorded answers and applies the difference to your working tree. Review it like any other change:

  1. Inspect git diff — the update touches only files the template owns.
  2. Resolve any *.rej files: these are hunks that no longer applied cleanly because you modified the same lines. Apply the intent by hand, then delete the .rej.
  3. Run make check (Ruff, mypy, tests).
  4. Commit, e.g. chore: apply fastapi-bedrock template update.

docs.title: Excluding files you have diverged from
docs.text:
If you have rewritten a file and never want template updates to touch it again, add it to the skip list in .cruft.json:

{
  "template": "https://github.com/mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock",
  "skip": ["README.md", "Makefile"]
}

docs.title: Linking an existing project
docs.text:
Projects generated with plain cookiecutter have no .cruft.json, but you can adopt cruft after the fact:

uvx cruft link https://github.com/mohandoz/fastapi-bedrock

cruft asks for the answers you originally gave and which template commit the project matches; be accurate here or the first cruft update diff will be noisy.

docs.title: Changing answers later
docs.text: Answers are recorded in .cruft.json under context.cookiecutter. To change one (for example flipping use_observability on), edit the value and run uvx cruft update — the diff then includes everything that flag adds. Flags that remove modules work the same way in reverse, though you should verify nothing of yours imports the removed code.

docs.title: Release-to-release upgrade notes
docs.text: Template releases are tagged. The CHANGELOG and release notes describe what changed between tags, and the demo repository (a continuously rendered default configuration) lets you read tag-to-tag diffs of generated output — often the quickest way to see what an update will do to your project before running it.

docs.title: Initial migration compatibility
docs.text:
Freshly generated projects include an option-aware initial Alembic revision. If an older generated project already has any real file in migrations/versions/, do not graft the template's 2026-09-01_initial_schema.py in as a second base revision: keep your existing history and omit that incoming file from the cruft update. Add future model changes as normal forward revisions.

If an older project has no Alembic history but has a database created by local create_all, first compare that database with the current SQLModel metadata and establish a reviewed baseline for that existing schema. Applying the new create-table revision directly would fail on the existing tables; stamping an unverified schema would hide drift. New/empty databases can apply the shipped revision normally with make migrate.
